I only know how to use the built-in network like RNN of LSTM in PyTorch. But they tend to deal with every node in the previous layer that will give information to all nodes in the next layer.

I want to do something different but don't know how to code it myself. Like in this figure: the node a maps to all [d, e, f] three nodes in layer 2, while node b maps to [e,f] and node c only maps to [f]. As a result, node d will only contain information from a, while e will contain information from [a, b]. And f will contain information from all nodes in the previous layer. Does anyone know how to code this structure? PLS give me some insight I'll be very grateful :D

Structure

When you have a layer that looks like Fully-Connected layer but with custom connectivity, use a mask with proper structure.

Let's say x = [a, b, c] is your 3-dim input and W denotes the connectivity matrix.

>> x
tensor([[0.1825],
        [0.9598],
        [0.2871]])
>> W
tensor([[0.7459, 0.4669, 0.9687],
        [0.9016, 0.4690, 0.0471],
        [0.5926, 0.9700, 0.5222]])

then W[i][j] points to the connecting weight between jth input and ith output neuron. To build the structure similar to your toy example, we would make a mask like this

>> mask
tensor([[1., 0., 0.],
        [1., 1., 0.],
        [1., 1., 1.]])

Then you can simply mask the W

>> (mask * W) @ x
tensor([[0.1361],
        [0.6147],
        [1.1892]])

Note: @ is matrix multiplication and * is pointwise multiplication.

I'm afraid there's no way to do what you're asking for using the provided context. The closest thing would be [`torch.nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence.html), which allows you to pack sequences into a single tensor, but it doesn't allow you to specify which elements should be connected to which other elements.

I think you can achieve this by using `torch.nn.ModuleList` and manually computing the forward pass.

```
import torch

class MyModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.a = torch.nn.Linear(10, 5)
        self.b = torch.nn.Linear(10, 3)
        self.c = torch.nn.Linear(10, 2)

        self.d = torch.nn.Linear(5, 1)
        self.e = torch.nn.Linear(8, 1)
        self.f = torch.nn.Linear(7, 1)

        self.module_list = [self.a, self.b, self.c,
                            self.d, self.e, self.f]

    def forward(self, x):
        outputs = []
        for i, module in enumerate(self.module_list):
            if i == 0:
                output = module(x)
            elif i <= 2:
                output = module(x[:, i-1])
            else:
                # Concatenate the outputs of the first 3 layers
                concat_output = torch.cat([output, outputs[0], outputs[1], outputs[2]], dim=1)
                output = module(concat_output)
            outputs.append(output)
        return outputs[-1]
```

can someone tell me what the equivalent of tf.keras.Input() in pytorch is?

At the documentation it says, "Initiates a Keras Tensor", so does it just creates a new empty tensor?

Thanks

There's no equivalent in PyTorch to the Keras' Input. All you have to do is pass on the inputs as a tensor to the PyTorch model.

For eg: If you're working with a Conv net:


# Keras Code
input_image = Input(shape=(32,32,3)) # An input image of 32x32x3 (HxWxC)
feature = Conv2D(16, activation='relu', kernel_size=(3, 3))(input_image)

# PyTorch code
input_tensor = torch.randn(1, 3, 32, 32) # An input tensor of shape BatchSizexChannelsxHeightxWidth
feature = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=16, kernel_size=(2, 2))(input_tensor)

If it is a normal Dense layer:

# Keras
dense_input = Input(shape=(1,))
features = Dense(100)(dense_input)

# PyTorch
input_tensor = torch.tensor([10]) # A 1x1 tensor with value 10
features = nn.Linear(1, 100)(input_tensor)

The `tf.keras.Input` function is used to create an input layer for a model.
It can be used as follows:

```
input_layer = tf.keras.Input(shape=(32,))
x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu')(input_layer)
model = tf.keras.Model(inputs=input_layer, outputs=x)
```

In this example, `input_layer` is the input layer and `x` is the output layer.

---

**Update:**

As @jdehesa pointed out, you can also use `tf.keras.Input` to specify the shape of the input data (without creating a layer):

```
input_data = tf.random.normal((100, 32))
input_layer = tf.keras.Input(shape=(32,))
x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu')(input_layer)
model = tf.keras.Model(inputs=input_layer, outputs=x)

# This will raise an error because the input layer was not created with the correct shape:
model(input_data) # ValueError: Input 0 of node dense/MatMul was passed float32_ref from input_data:0 incompatible with expected type bool

# But if we change the shape of the input layer...
input_layer = tf.keras.Input(shape=(32,), dtype=tf.float32)
x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu')(input_layer)
model = tf.keras.Model(inputs=input_layer, outputs=x)

# ...it works!
model(input_data) # <tf.Tensor 'dense/BiasAdd:0' shape=(100, 64) dtype=float32>
```

I have a rather quick question on tensordot operation. I'm trying to figure out if there is a way to perform a tensordot product between two tensors to get the right output of shape that I want. One of the tensors is B X L X D dimensions and the other one is B X 1 X D dimensions and I'm trying to figure out if it's possible to end up with B X D matrix at the end.

Currently I'm looping through the B dimension and performing a matrix multiplication between 1 X D and D X L (transposing L X D) matrices and stacking them to end up with B X L matrix at the end. This is obviously not the fastest way possible as a loop can be expensive. Would it be possible to get the desired output of B X D shape by performing a quick tensordot? I cannot seem to figure out a way to get rid of 1 of the B's.

Any insight or direction would be very much appreciated.

One option

Is to use torch.bmm() which does exactly that (docs).

It takes tensors of shape (b, n, m) and (b, m, p) and returns the batch matrix multiplication of shape (b, n, p).

(I assume you ment a result of B X L since the matrix multiplication of 1 X D and D X L is of shape 1 X L and not 1 X D).

In your case:

import torch
B, L, D = 32, 10, 512

a = torch.randn(B, 1, D)    #shape (B X 1 X D)
b = torch.randn(B, L, D)    #shape (B X L X D)

b = b.transpose(1,2)        #shape (B X D X L)

result = torch.bmm(a, b)

result = result.squeeze()
print(result.shape)
>>> torch.Size([32, 10])

Alternatively

You can use torch.einsum(), which is more compact but less readable in my opinion:

import torch
B, L, D = 32, 10, 512

a = torch.randn(B, 1, D)
b = torch.randn(B, L, D)

result = torch.einsum('abc, adc->ad', a, b)

print(result.shape)
>>> torch.Size([32, 10])

The squeeze at the end is in order to make your result of shape (32, 10) instead of shape (32, 1, 10).

I think you're looking for [`torch.einsum`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.einsum.html):

```
import torch

a = torch.rand(2, 3, 4)
b = torch.rand(2, 1, 4)

c = torch.einsum('bij,bkj->bik', a, b)
print(c.shape)  # torch.Size([2, 3, 1])
```

The string `'bij,bkj->bik'` specifies how the indices should be matched:

- `b` is repeated so it matches across the batch dimension
- `i` is present in the first tensor but not the second, so it is summed over
- `j` is present in the second tensor but not the first, so it is summed over
- `k` is present in neither tensor, so it is kept as-is

This is equivalent to:

```
c = torch.zeros(a.size(0), a.size(1), b.size(2))

for i in range(a.size(0)):
    for j in range(b.size(0)):
        c[i] += torch.mm(a[i].mm(b[j]), torch.ones(a.size(2)))
```

which is equivalent to:

```
c = torch.bmm(a, b.expand_as(a)).squeeze()
```

but without any loops.

### Division by Zero in Autograd 

When performing division by zero in PyTorch (e.g., `x / 0`  ), the forward pass will produce `inf`  values following IEEE-754 floating point arithmetic. While these `inf`  values can be masked out before computing the final loss (e.g., via indexing or masking), the autograd system still tracks and differentiates through the full computation graph, including the division by zero operation. 

During backpropagation, this can lead to problematic gradient expressions. For example: 

```
x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

y = x / div          # Results in [inf, 1]
mask = div != 0      # [False, True]
loss = y[mask].sum()
loss.backward()
print(x.grad)        # [nan, 1], not [0, 1]

```

In this example, even though we only use the masked output (which excludes the division by zero), autograd still computes gradients through the full computation graph, including the division by zero operation. This results in `nan`  gradients for the masked elements, which can cause training instability. 

To avoid this issue, there are several recommended approaches: 

1. Mask before division:

```
x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

mask = div != 0
safe = torch.zeros_like(x)
safe[mask] = x[mask] / div[mask]
loss = safe.sum()
loss.backward()      # Produces safe gradients [0, 1]

```

2. Use MaskedTensor (experimental API):

```
from torch.masked import as_masked_tensor

x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

The main difference is that `torch.tensor` will copy the input tensor by default (unless you pass `share_memory=True`). On the other hand, `.clone()` and `.detach()` do not copy the tensor unless it's necessary.

g = e.detach()
h = f.clone()

assert id(b) != id(a)
assert id(c) == id(a)
assert id(d) == id(a)

of `input`  . Otherwise, it will be a copy. Contiguous inputs and inputs
with compatible strides can be reshaped without copying, but you should not
depend on the copying vs. viewing behavior. 

See [`torch.Tensor.view()`](torch.Tensor.view.html#torch.Tensor.view "torch.Tensor.view")  on when it is possible to return a view. 

A single dimension may be -1, in which case it’s inferred from the remaining
dimensions and the number of elements in `input`  .

Example: 

```
>>> a = torch.arange(4.)
>>> torch.reshape(a, (2, 2))
tensor([[ 0.,  1.],
        [ 2.,  3.]])
>>> b = torch.tensor([[0, 1], [2, 3]])
>>> torch.reshape(b, (-1,))

To fix this, you need to pass a batch of samples through your network. You can do this by simply changing the first dimension of your input tensors:

At the heart of PyTorch data loading utility is the [`torch.utils.data.DataLoader`](#torch.utils.data.DataLoader "torch.utils.data.DataLoader")  class. It represents a Python iterable over a dataset, with support for 

* [map-style and iterable-style datasets](#dataset-types)  ,
* [customizing data loading order](#data-loading-order-and-sampler)  ,
* [automatic batching](#loading-batched-and-non-batched-data)  ,
* [single- and multi-process data loading](#single-and-multi-process-data-loading)  ,
* [automatic memory pinning](#memory-pinning)  .

These options are configured by the constructor arguments of a [`DataLoader`](#torch.utils.data.DataLoader "torch.utils.data.DataLoader")  , which has signature: 

```
DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=1, shuffle=False, sampler=None,
           batch_sampler=None, num_workers=0, collate_fn=None,
           pin_memory=False, drop_last=False, timeout=0,
           worker_init_fn=None, *, prefetch_factor=2,
           persistent_workers=False)

```

The sections below describe in details the effects and usages of these options. 

Dataset Types 
--------------------------------------------------------------

The most important argument of [`DataLoader`](#torch.utils.data.DataLoader "torch.utils.data.DataLoader")  constructor is [`dataset`](utils.html#module-torch.utils.data.dataset "torch.utils.data.dataset")  , which indicates a dataset object to load data
from. PyTorch supports two different types of datasets:

---

### Single-process data loading (default) 

In this mode, data fetching is done in the same process a [`DataLoader`](#torch.utils.data.DataLoader "torch.utils.data.DataLoader")  is initialized. Therefore, data loading
may block computing. However, this mode may be preferred when resource(s) used
for sharing data among processes (e.g., shared memory, file descriptors) is
limited, or when the entire dataset is small and can be loaded entirely in
memory. Additionally, single-process loading often shows more readable error
traces and thus is useful for debugging.

The `CyclicLR` is not changing the learning rate of your optimizer directly. Instead, it updates the learning rates of the optimizer's parameter groups.

When you call `scheduler.step()`, the `CyclicLR` will update its internal state based on the current epoch or iteration count. Then, when you call `optimizer.step()` after computing the gradients, the `CyclicLR` will update the learning rates of the optimizer's parameter groups.

So, the `CyclicLR` is not overwriting the optimizer, but rather updating the learning rates of the optimizer's parameter groups. The optimizer is still responsible for applying the updated learning rates to the parameters during optimization.

Example 

```
>>> model = torch.nn.Linear(10, 10)
>>> optim = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4)
>>> scheduler1 = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LinearLR(
...     optim,
...     start_factor=0.1,
...     end_factor=1,
...     total_iters=20,
... )
>>> scheduler2 = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(
...     optim,
...     T_max=80,
...     eta_min=3e-5,
... )
>>> lr = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.SequentialLR(
...     optim,
...     schedulers=[scheduler1, scheduler2],
...     milestones=[20],
... )
>>> lr.load_state_dict(torch.load("./save_seq.pt"))
>>> # now load the optimizer checkpoint after loading the LRScheduler
>>> optim.load_state_dict(torch.load("./save_optim.pt"))

```

The `logits` returned by the model are the raw scores before any activation function is applied. In this case, you're using a classification head which has two linear layers followed by a softmax layer.

In general, the final layer of a classifier will be a linear layer that maps from the hidden state dimension to the number of classes. For BERT, this is typically 2 for binary classification tasks like sentiment analysis. The output of this layer is then passed through a softmax function to get the probabilities of each class.

So in your case, the `logits` are the raw scores before the softmax is applied. To get the probabilities, you need to apply the softmax function to the `logits`. This will give you the probabilities of each class.

As for what the classes represent, it depends on the task. In the case of sentiment analysis, the classes might be "positive" and "negative". In the case of named entity recognition, the classes might be different types of entities like "person", "organization", etc.

```
>>> transformer_model = nn.Transformer(nhead=16, num_encoder_layers=12)

Batch Normalization layer has different behavior in training vs. inferencing:

  1. During training (i.e. when using fit() or when calling the layer/model with the argument training=True), the layer normalizes its output using the mean and standard deviation of the current batch of inputs.

  2. During inference (i.e. when using evaluate() or predict() or when calling the layer/model with the argument training=False (which is the default), the layer normalizes its output using a moving average of the mean and standard deviation of the batches it has seen during training.

So, the first result is due to default training=False and the second is due to default is_training=True.

The difference between the two implementations comes from the fact that Keras uses `momentum=0.99` by default while TensorFlow uses `decay=0.99` by default.
This means that the running mean and variance will be updated differently.

First you need to understand the ranks. To be brief: in a multiprocessing context we typically assume that rank 0 is the first process or base process. The other processes are then ranked differently, e.g. 1, 2, 3, totalling four processes in total.

Some operations are not necessary to be done in parallel or you just need one process to do some preprocessing or caching so that the other processes can use that data.

In your example, if the first if statement is entered by the non-base processes (rank 1, 2, 3), they will block (or "wait") because they run into the barrier. They wait there, because barrier() blocks until all processes have reached a barrier, but the base process has not reached a barrier yet.

So at this point the non-base processes (1, 2, 3) are blocked, but the base process (0) continues. The base process will do some operations (preprocess and cache data, in this case) until it reaches the second if-statement. There, the base process will run into a barrier. At this point, all processes have stopped at a barrier, meaning that all current barriers can be lifted and all processes can continue. Because the base process prepared the data, the other processes can now use that data.

Perhaps the most important thing to understand is:

  • when a process encounters a barrier it will block
  • the position of the barrier is not important (not all processes have to enter the same if-statement, for instance)
  • a process is blocked by a barrier until all processes have encountered a barrier, upon which those barriers are lifted for all processes

The `barrier` is there to ensure that all workers have finished their tasks before proceeding with the next one.

In the first case, the barrier ensures that all workers have finished preprocessing the data before any worker starts saving the preprocessed data. This is necessary because the saving operation is done by the master worker (local rank 0), so we need to make sure that all other workers have finished their task before starting the saving operation.

In the second case, the barrier ensures that all workers have finished loading the model and the vocabulary before any worker starts using them. This is necessary because the model and the vocabulary are loaded by the master worker (local rank 0), so we need to make sure that all other workers have finished their task before starting using the model and the vocabulary.

The error you're getting is because `cv2.imread` returns a numpy array, not a `cv2.UMat`. You can fix this by changing your `cv2.imread` call to:

```
image = cv2.imread(input_path+rows['ID'], flags=cv2.IMREAD_UNCHANGED)

However, there's no need to use OpenCV at all here. You can just use Python's built-in file handling functions to save the files. Here's a complete example that should work for you:

```
import os
from shutil import copyfile
import pandas as pd

# Load the dataframe from csv
df_features = pd.read_csv('meta.csv')

# Create the destination directory if it doesn't exist
dest_path = input_path + 'imageProcessDir'
if not os.path.exists(dest_path):
    os.makedirs(dest_path)

# Iterate over the dataframe
for index, rows in df_features.iterrows():
    # Get the source path
    src_path = os.path.join(input_path, 'imgs', rows['ID'])

    # Get the destination path
    dest_folder = os.path.join(dest_path, rows['PatientID'])
    if not os.path.exists(dest_folder):
        os.makedirs(dest_folder)
    dest_path = os.path.join(dest_folder, rows['ID'] + '_' + str(index) + '.dcm')

    # Copy the file
    copyfile(src_path, dest_path)

Moreover, as for [`gather()`](torch.Tensor.gather.html#torch.Tensor.gather "torch.Tensor.gather")  , the values of `index`  must be

I'm afraid there's no way to control the precision of printing tensors in pytorch. The best solution would be to convert your tensor into numpy array before printing:

```
import torch
a = torch.rand(10)
print(a.numpy()) # this will print floats with default precision
```

Or you could define your own function to print tensors with desired precision:

```
def print_tensor(t, precision):
    print(" ".join(f"{x:.{precision}f}" for x in t))
```

And then call it like so:

```
print_tensor(a, 4)
```

The `precision` argument only affects the number of digits printed, not whether or not trailing zeroes are included.

If you want to include them, you can use the `float_format` argument:

```
>>> import torch
>>> x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.3456789, 3.141592653589793])
>>> torch.set_printoptions(float_format='{:f}'.format)
>>> print(x)
tensor([1.000000, 2.345679, 3.141593])
```

Example: 

```

>>> torch.set_printoptions(precision=2)

>>> torch.arange(10)

You can not parallelize RNN in time (1000 here) because they are inherently sequential.

You can use a light RNN, something like QRNN or SRU as a faster alternative(which is still sequential).

Another common sequence processing modules are TCN and Transformers which are both parallelizable in time.

Also, note that all of them can be used with attention and work perfectly fine with text.

I think you can use the same approach as in the translation example.
The main difference is that your input sequence will have variable length (the number of words in each document) while the output sequence has fixed length (the number of words in the summary).
So, instead of using `pack_padded_sequence` you should use `pad_packed_sequence`.
Here's some code:

```
import torch.nn as nn

class Seq2Seq(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, encoder, decoder):
        super(Seq2Seq, self).__init__()
        self.encoder = encoder
        self.decoder = decoder

    def forward(self, src, trg):
        # src: [src_len, batch_size]
        # trg: [trg_len, batch_size]

        embedded = self.encoder(src)
        # embedded: [src_len, batch_size, hidden_dim]

        context_vector = self.encoder.get_context_vector(embedded)
        # context_vector: [batch_size, hidden_dim]

        output = self.decoder(context_vector, trg)
        # output: [trg_len, batch_size, vocab_size]

        return output

If you insist on training a network on this mixed dataset, you can either

From training a neural network point of view, the first option makes more sense. This can be achieved by averaging a color image across the RGB channel.

The key points are:

The problem is that your `__getitem__` method returns two different types of objects:

```
def __getitem__(self, idx):
    ...
    return image, label
```

In particular, `image` is a `torch.Tensor`, while `label` is an integer.

When you pass your custom dataset to a [`DataLoader`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html#torch.utils.data.DataLoader), it will try to collate the batches using the [`collate_fn`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html#data-loading-utils). By default, the `collate_fn` tries to stack the elements along the first dimension. This fails because the tensors have different sizes.

To fix this, you need to provide a custom `collate_fn`. You can do this by passing a function to the `collate_fn` argument of the `DataLoader`.

For example, you could use something like this:

```
def collate_fn(batch):
    images, labels = zip(*batch)
    return torch.stack(images), torch.tensor(labels)
```

This will convert the tuples returned by `__getitem__` into lists, which can then be converted into tensors. Note that this assumes that the labels are integers. If they are not, you should modify the code accordingly.

In this case, loading from a map-style dataset is roughly equivalent with: 

```
for indices in batch_sampler:
    yield collate_fn([dataset[i] for i in indices])

```

and loading from an iterable-style dataset is roughly equivalent with: 

```
dataset_iter = iter(dataset)
for indices in batch_sampler:
    yield collate_fn([next(dataset_iter) for _ in indices])

```

A custom `collate_fn`  can be used to customize collation, e.g., padding
sequential data to max length of a batch. See [this section](#dataloader-collate-fn)  on more about `collate_fn`  .

The `Trainer` class is a wrapper around the `DataLoader`, `model`, `optimizer`, etc. that you can pass to your training loop.

In particular, the `Trainer` class will call the `train()` function of the `DataLoader`. The `DataLoader` will then call the `__iter__()` function of the `Dataset` object that you pass to the `DataLoader`.

This means that the `Trainer` class doesn't know anything about the `Dataset` object that you pass to the `DataLoader`. All it knows is that the `Dataset` object implements the `__len__()` and `__getitem__()` methods.

Therefore, when you create an instance of the `Trainer` class, you don't need to worry about how the `DataLoader` will get the data from the `Dataset` object. You just need to make sure that the `Dataset` object implements the required methods.

As for why the `Trainer` class passes the `labels` argument instead of the `label` one, I'm afraid I don't have enough information to answer that.

Prior versions of PyTorch allowed certain pointwise functions to execute on tensors with different shapes,
as long as the number of elements in each tensor was equal. The pointwise operation would then be carried
out by viewing each tensor as 1-dimensional. PyTorch now supports broadcasting and the “1-dimensional”
pointwise behavior is considered deprecated and will generate a Python warning in cases where tensors are
not broadcastable, but have the same number of elements. 

Note that the introduction of broadcasting can cause backwards incompatible changes in the case where
two tensors do not have the same shape, but are broadcastable and have the same number of elements.
For Example: 

```
>>> torch.add(torch.ones(4,1), torch.randn(4))

```

would previously produce a Tensor with size: torch.Size([4,1]), but now produces a Tensor with size: torch.Size([4,4]).
In order to help identify cases in your code where backwards incompatibilities introduced by broadcasting may exist,
you may set *torch.utils.backcompat.broadcast_warning.enabled* to *True* , which will generate a python warning
in such cases.

I'm afraid this is not possible. Backpropagation is always done through the entire computation graph, even if some intermediate results are unused. This is because the gradients of those intermediate results may still be needed later in the computation graph.

The problem with your code is that you're doing `x *= gate_A` instead of `x = x * gate_A`. The first operation doesn't do anything because it's equivalent to `x = x * gate_A`, but `*=` is an inplace operation, so it will update the memory address of `x` to point to the result of the multiplication, while `*` returns a new tensor.

This means that when you call `backward()` on the loss, only the last tensor that was updated in-place will have its gradient computed, and the rest won't. This is why you don't see any difference in performance between the two cases.

If you want to keep track of the original tensors, you should use [`torch.where`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.where.html#torch.where), like this:

```
def forward(self, x):
    # Only one gate is supposed to be enabled at random
    # However, for the experiment, I fixed the values to [1,0] and [1,1]
    choice  =  randint(0,1)
    gate_A  =  torch.tensor(choice   ,dtype = torch.bool) 
    gate_B  =  torch.tensor(1-choice ,dtype = torch.bool) 

    a = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv1a(x)))
    a = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv2a(a)))

    b = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv1b(x)))
    b = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv2b(b)))

    a = torch.where(gate_A, a, torch.zeros_like(a))
    b = torch.where(gate_B, b, torch.zeros_like(b))

    x  = torch.cat( [a,b], dim = 1 )

    x = torch.flatten(x, 1) # flatten all dimensions except batch
    x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
    x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
    x = self.fc3(x)
    return x
```

The first version is correct.

`zero_grad()` clears out the gradients computed from the last step. If you don't do this, the gradient would be accumulated to existing gradients.

So if you run `backward()` multiple times on different batches (without calling `zero_grad()`), the gradients will keep accumulating and eventually give you an incorrect optimization result.

The default behavior (letting `.grad`  s be `None`  before the first `backward()`  , such that their layout is created according to 1 or 2,
and retained over time according to 3 or 4) is recommended for best performance.
Calls to `model.zero_grad()`  or `optimizer.zero_grad()`  will not affect `.grad`  layouts. 

In fact, resetting all `.grad`  s to `None`  before each
accumulation phase, e.g.: 

```
for iterations...
    ...
    for param in model.parameters():
        param.grad = None
    loss.backward()

```

such that they’re recreated according to 1 or 2 every time,
is a valid alternative to `model.zero_grad()`  or `optimizer.zero_grad()`  that may improve performance for some networks.

I'm not sure how to help you without knowing your model architecture. However, here's a general guide on how to debug such issues:

1. Check the shapes of all tensors involved in the computation. In particular, check whether the number of channels matches between the convolutional layer and the input tensor.
2. Try to reproduce the problem using fewer layers. For example, try removing one layer at a time until the problem disappears. This should allow you to identify which layer is causing the problem.
3. If you've narrowed down the problem to a single layer, try printing intermediate outputs of the layer. You may find that the layer is producing unexpected results.

The problem is that you're using `nn.Conv2d` twice without any change in the number of channels.

```
nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
nn.Conv2d(32, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
```

This will make your first layer take an input of shape `[batch_size, 3, height, width]`, and then produce an output of shape `[batch_size, 32, height, width]`. The second layer expects an input of shape `[batch_size, 32, height, width]`, but you give it an input of shape `[batch_size, 64, height, width]`.

To fix this, you need to add another channel dimension between these two layers. You can do this by adding a `nn.Conv2d` layer with `in_channels=32` and `out_channels=64`:

```
nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
```

Discriminator's job is to perform Binary Classification to detect between Real and Fake so its loss function is Binary Cross Entropy.

What Generator does is Density Estimation, from the noise to real data, and feed it to Discriminator to fool it.

The approach followed in the design is to model it as MinMax game. Now let's have a look at cost functions:

Someone explained this as:

The first term in J(D) represents feeding the actual data to the discriminator, and the discriminator would want to maximize the log probability of predicting one, indicating that the data is real. The second term represents the samples generated by G. Here, the discriminator would want to maximize the log probability of predicting zero, indicating the the data is fake. The generator, on the other hand tries to minimize the log probability of the discriminator being correct. The solution to this problem is an equilibrium point of the game, which is a saddle point of the discriminator loss.

Since the Discriminator tries to maximize the probability of Generator's sample as Zero, the Generator's job becomes to maximize for one. This is equivalent to making the Generator’s cost function the negative cross entropy, where the first term in J(D) would now be constant.

### Division by Zero in Autograd 

When performing division by zero in PyTorch (e.g., `x / 0`  ), the forward pass will produce `inf`  values following IEEE-754 floating point arithmetic. While these `inf`  values can be masked out before computing the final loss (e.g., via indexing or masking), the autograd system still tracks and differentiates through the full computation graph, including the division by zero operation. 

During backpropagation, this can lead to problematic gradient expressions. For example: 

```
x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

y = x / div          # Results in [inf, 1]
mask = div != 0      # [False, True]
loss = y[mask].sum()
loss.backward()
print(x.grad)        # [nan, 1], not [0, 1]

```

In this example, even though we only use the masked output (which excludes the division by zero), autograd still computes gradients through the full computation graph, including the division by zero operation. This results in `nan`  gradients for the masked elements, which can cause training instability. 

To avoid this issue, there are several recommended approaches: 

1. Mask before division:

```
x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

mask = div != 0
safe = torch.zeros_like(x)
safe[mask] = x[mask] / div[mask]
loss = safe.sum()
loss.backward()      # Produces safe gradients [0, 1]

```

2. Use MaskedTensor (experimental API):

```
from torch.masked import as_masked_tensor

x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

If your train script works with `torch.distributed.launch`  it will continue
working with `torchrun`  with these differences: 

1. No need to manually pass `RANK`  , `WORLD_SIZE`  , `MASTER_ADDR`  , and `MASTER_PORT`  .
2. `rdzv_backend`  and `rdzv_endpoint`  can be provided. For most users
this will be set to `c10d`  (see [rendezvous](rendezvous.html)  ). The default `rdzv_backend`  creates a non-elastic rendezvous where `rdzv_endpoint`  holds
the master address.
3. Make sure you have a `load_checkpoint(path)`  and `save_checkpoint(path)`  logic in your script. When any number of
workers fail we restart all the workers with the same program
arguments so you will lose progress up to the most recent checkpoint
(see [elastic launch](run.html)  ).
4. `use_env`  flag has been removed. If you were parsing local rank by parsing
the `--local-rank`  option, you need to get the local rank from the
environment variable `LOCAL_RANK`  (e.g. `int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])`  ).

### Dynamic shape operations (nonzero and friends) 

`vmap(f)`  requires that `f`  applied to every “example” in your input
returns a Tensor with the same shape. Operations such as `torch.nonzero`  , `torch.is_nonzero`  are not supported and will error as a result. 

To see why, consider the following example: 

```
xs = torch.tensor([[0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 3]])
vmap(torch.nonzero)(xs)

```

`torch.nonzero(xs[0])`  returns a Tensor of shape 2;
but `torch.nonzero(xs[1])`  returns a Tensor of shape 1.
We are unable to construct a single Tensor as an output;
the output would need to be a ragged Tensor (and PyTorch does not yet have
the concept of a ragged Tensor).

Randomness 
--------------------------------------------------------

The user’s intention when calling a random operation can be unclear. Specifically, some users may want
the random behavior to be the same across batches while others may want it to differ across batches.
To address this, `vmap`  takes a randomness flag. 

The flag can only be passed to vmap and can take on 3 values, “error,” “different,” or “same,” defaulting
to error. Under “error” mode, any call to a random function will produce an error asking the user to use
one of the other two flags based on their use case. 

Under “different” randomness, elements in a batch produce different random values. For instance, 

```
def add_noise(x):
  y = torch.randn(())  # y will be different across the batch
  return x + y

x = torch.ones(3)
result = vmap(add_noise, randomness="different")(x)  # we get 3 different values

```

torch::Tensor square_cpu(torch::Tensor input) {
    // Check that input is a CPU tensor
    TORCH_CHECK(input.device().is_cpu(), "Input must be a CPU tensor");

    // Create output tensor with same shape and dtype as input
    torch::Tensor output = torch::empty_like(input);

    // For loop to compute square of each element

:   Creates a 1-dimensional [`Tensor`](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor")  from an object that implements

Skips the first `offset`  bytes in the buffer, and interprets the rest of
the raw bytes as a 1-dimensional tensor of type [`dtype`](../tensor_attributes.html#torch.dtype "torch.dtype")  with `count`  elements. 

Note that either of the following must be true: 

1. `count`  is a positive non-zero number, and the total number of bytes
in the buffer is more than `offset`  plus `count`  times the size
(in bytes) of [`dtype`](../tensor_attributes.html#torch.dtype "torch.dtype")  . 

2. `count`  is negative, and the length (number of bytes) of the buffer
subtracted by the `offset`  is a multiple of the size (in bytes) of [`dtype`](../tensor_attributes.html#torch.dtype "torch.dtype")  . 

The returned tensor and buffer share the same memory. Modifications to
the tensor will be reflected in the buffer and vice versa. The returned
tensor is not resizable. 

Note

owns the shared memory. Therefore, such memory will not be deallocated

### What does the error mean?

The error means that you're trying to create a new process while another process is still being created. This happens because you're trying to create a new process inside a subprocess, which is not allowed.

### How do I fix it?

There are two ways to fix this:

1. Don't use multiprocessing in a subprocess. You can do this by moving the multiprocessing code outside of the subprocess.
2. Use `if __name__ == "__main__":`. This is necessary because Python needs to be able to import the module containing the multiprocessing code, so it creates a new process to do that. But since the new process already exists, it cannot create any new processes itself. By putting the multiprocessing code under `if __name__ == "__main__":`, you ensure that the code is only executed in the main process, not in the subprocesses.

So, assuming that your code looks something like this:

```python
import multiprocessing

def worker():
    pass

if __name__ == "__main__":
    pool = multiprocessing.Pool(processes=4)
    pool.map(worker, range(100))
```

You need to move the multiprocessing code outside of the subprocess:

```
import multiprocessing

def worker():
    pass

if __name__ == "__main__":
    pool = multiprocessing.Pool(processes=4)
    pool.map(worker, range(100))

subprocess.run(["python", "-c", "print('Hello world')"])
```

Or, alternatively, you could put the multiprocessing code under `if __name__ == "__main__":`:

```
import multiprocessing

def worker():
    pass

if __name__ == "__main__":
    pool = multiprocessing.Pool(processes=4)
    pool.map(worker, range(100))
    subprocess.run(["python", "-c", "print('Hello world')"])
```

Either way, the error should go away.

To solve this issue, you need to set `num_workers=0`. This will disable the use of subprocesses and instead use threads. Since your dataset is small enough to fit into memory, this should work just fine. If your dataset is too large, you may want to look at [this](https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/using-multiprocessing-with-large-datasets/915).

I've looked a bit into this tonight. I don't have a solution (edit: I have a mitigation, see the edit at end), but I have a bit more information.

It seems the issue is caused by NVidia fatbins (.nv_fatb) being loaded into memory. Several DLLs, such as cusolver64_xx.dll, torcha_cuda_cu.dll, and a few others, have .nv_fatb sections in them. These contain tons of different variations of CUDA code for different GPUs, so it ends up being several hundred megabytes to a couple gigabytes.

When Python imports 'torch' it loads these DLLs, and maps the .nv_fatb section into memory. For some reason, instead of just being a memory mapped file, it is actually taking up memory. The section is set as 'copy on write', so it's possible something writes into it? I don't know. But anyway, if you look at Python using VMMap ( https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/vmmap ) you can see that these DLLs are committing huge amounts of committed memory for this .nv_fatb section. The frustrating part is it doesn't seem to be using the memory. For example, right now my Python.exe has 2.7GB committed, but the working set is only 148MB.

Every Python process that loads these DLLs will commit several GB of memory loading these DLLs. So if 1 Python process is wasting 2GB of memory, and you try running 8 workers, you need 16GB of memory to spare just to load the DLLs. It really doesn't seem like this memory is used, just committed.

I don't know enough about these fatbinaries to try to fix it, but from looking at this for the past 2 hours it really seems like they are the issue. Perhaps its an NVidia problem that these are committing memory?

edit: I made this python script: https://gist.github.com/cobryan05/7d1fe28dd370e110a372c4d268dcb2e5

Get it and install its pefile dependency ( python -m pip install pefile ).

Run it on your torch and cuda DLLs. In OPs case, command line might look like:

python fixNvPe.py --input=C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python38\lib\site-packages\torch\lib\*.dll

(You also want to run this wherever your cusolver64_*.dll and friends are. This may be in your torch\lib folder, or it may be, eg, C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\vXX.X\bin . If it is under Program Files, you will need to run the script with administrative privileges)

What this script is going to do is scan through all DLLs specified by the input glob, and if it finds an .nv_fatb section it will back up the DLL, disable ASLR, and mark the .nv_fatb section read-only.

ASLR is 'address space layout randomization.' It is a security feature that randomizes where a DLL is loaded in memory. We disable it for this DLL so that all Python processes will load the DLL into the same base virtual address. If all Python processes using the DLL load it at the same base address, they can all share the DLL. Otherwise each process needs its own copy.

Marking the section 'read-only' lets Windows know that the contents will not change in memory. If you map a file into memory read/write, Windows has to commit enough memory, backed by the pagefile, just in case you make a modification to it. If the section is read-only, there is no need to back it in the pagefile. We know there are no modifications to it, so it can always be found in the DLL.

The theory behind the script is that by changing these 2 flags that less memory will be committed for the .nv_fatb, and more memory will be shared between the Python processes. In practice, it works. Not quite as well as I'd hope (it still commits a lot more than it uses), so my understanding may be flawed, but it significantly decreases memory commit.

In my limited testing I haven't ran into any issues, but I can't guarantee there are no code paths that attempts to write to that section we marked 'read only.' If you start running into issues, though, you can just restore the backups.

edit 2022-01-20: Per NVIDIA: "We have gone ahead and marked the nv_fatb section as read-only, this change will be targeting next major CUDA release 11.7 . We are not changing the ASLR, as that is considered a safety feature ."

This should certainly help. If it's not enough without ASLR as well then the script should still work

This section will go over some of the Dynamo internals and will

### Backend/Hardware Support 

| Hardware | Kernel Library | Eager Mode Quantization | FX Graph Mode Quantization | Quantization Mode Support |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| server CPU | fbgemm/onednn | Supported | | All Supported |
| mobile CPU | qnnpack/xnnpack | | |
| server GPU | TensorRT (early prototype) | Not support this it requires a graph | Supported | Static Quantization |

Today, PyTorch supports the following backends for running quantized operators efficiently: 

* x86 CPUs with AVX2 support or higher (without AVX2 some operations have inefficient implementations), via *x86* optimized by [fbgemm](https://github.com/pytorch/FBGEMM)  and [onednn](https://github.com/oneapi-src/oneDNN)  (see the details at [RFC](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/83888)  )
* ARM CPUs (typically found in mobile/embedded devices), via [qnnpack](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/main/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qnnpack)
* (early prototype) support for NVidia GPU via [TensorRT](https://developer.nvidia.com/tensorrt)  through *fx2trt* (to be open sourced)

#### Note for native CPU backends 

We expose both *x86* and *qnnpack* with the same native pytorch quantized operators, so we need additional flag to distinguish between them. The corresponding implementation of *x86* and *qnnpack* is chosen automatically based on the PyTorch build mode, though users have the option to override this by setting *torch.backends.quantization.engine* to *x86* or *qnnpack* .

Yes, you're right. Usually, for running loss the term

total_loss+= loss.item()*15

is written instead as (as done in transfer learning tutorial)

total_loss+= loss.item()*images.size(0)

where images.size(0) gives the current batch size. Thus, it'll give 10 (in your case) instead of hard-coded 15 for the last batch. loss.item()*len(images) is also correct!

In your second example, since you're using reduction='sum', the loss won't be divided by the batch size as it's done by default (because, by default, the reduction='mean' i.e. losses are averaged across observations for each minibatch).

Note that `torch.mean` is used instead of `torch.sum`. This is because the loss should be averaged over the batch size.

The `reduction` argument of [`F.cross_entropy`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy.html#torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy) is used to specify what should be done with the losses computed for each element in the batch.

- `'mean'`: The mean of the losses is returned.
- `'sum'`: The sum of the losses is returned.
- `'none'`: No reduction is applied, so the output tensor has the same shape as the input one.

In your case, you want to compute the average loss per image over an epoch, so you can set `reduction='mean'`. This way, the loss returned by `F.cross_entropy` will already be divided by the number of elements in the batch, so there's no need to do this manually.

```
total_loss += loss.item() * len(images)
```

Note that if you set `reduction='sum'`, then you would need to divide by the number of elements in the batch:

```
total_loss += loss.item()
avg_loss_per_epoch = total_loss / len(train_set)

The problem here is that you're trying to apply a `Conv2D` layer on a tensor of size `(3, 100, 10)`.

This is wrong because:

- The first dimension should be the number of input channels, so it should be `3`.
- The second and third dimensions should be the height and width of your input image respectively, so they should be `100` and `10`.

So, you need to change the shape of your input tensor from `(3, 100, 10)` to `(3, 100, 10)`.

Here's how you can do it:

```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class Net(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=6, kernel_size=(5, 5))
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=6, out_channels=16, kernel_size=(5, 5))

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_features=864, out_features=120)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(in_features=120, out_features=84)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(in_features=84, out_features=2)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.relu(self.conv1(x))
        x = F.max_pool2d(x, 2)
        x = F.relu(self.conv2(x))
        x = F.max_pool2d(x, 2)
        x = x.view(-1, 864)
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
        x = self.fc3(x)

        return x

net = Net()

# Your input tensor
x = torch.randn(3, 100, 10)

# Reshape the tensor
x = x.unsqueeze(0)

# Pass the reshaped tensor through the network
output = net(x)

You are forgetting the "minibatch dimension", each "1D" sample has indeed two dimensions: the number of channels (7 in your example) and length (10 in your case). However, pytorch expects as input not a single sample, but rather a minibatch of B samples stacked together along the "minibatch dimension".
So a "1D" CNN in pytorch expects a 3D tensor as input: BxCxT. If you only have one signal, you can add a singleton dimension:

 out = model(torch.tensor(X)[None, ...])

I think you need to reshape your input tensor `X` into a 3D tensor before passing it to the network:

```
X = X.reshape(1, 7, -1)
```

This way, the first dimension represents the batch size, the second one the number of channels and the third one the length of the sequence.

The problem is that you're passing a 2D tensor to your network, while it expects a 3D one.

In order to fix it, you need to add another dimension to your input:

```
X = X.unsqueeze(0) # or X = X[None]

Backwards compatibility 
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Prior versions of PyTorch allowed certain pointwise functions to execute on tensors with different shapes,
as long as the number of elements in each tensor was equal. The pointwise operation would then be carried
out by viewing each tensor as 1-dimensional. PyTorch now supports broadcasting and the “1-dimensional”
pointwise behavior is considered deprecated and will generate a Python warning in cases where tensors are
not broadcastable, but have the same number of elements. 

Note that the introduction of broadcasting can cause backwards incompatible changes in the case where
two tensors do not have the same shape, but are broadcastable and have the same number of elements.
For Example: 

```
>>> torch.add(torch.ones(4,1), torch.randn(4))

```

would previously produce a Tensor with size: torch.Size([4,1]), but now produces a Tensor with size: torch.Size([4,4]).
In order to help identify cases in your code where backwards incompatibilities introduced by broadcasting may exist,
you may set *torch.utils.backcompat.broadcast_warning.enabled* to *True* , which will generate a python warning
in such cases.

The embedding layer is not supposed to change during training. The weights of the embedding layer are learned parameters that are updated by backpropagation.

If you want to use pretrained embeddings, you can set `requires_grad=False` on the embedding layer so that it won't be updated during training. You can do this after loading your pretrained embeddings:

embedding.weight.data.copy_(pretrained_embeddings)
embedding.weight.requires_grad = False

AdaptiveLogSoftmaxWithLoss 
========================================================================================

*class* torch.nn. AdaptiveLogSoftmaxWithLoss ( *in_features*  , *n_classes*  , *cutoffs*  , *div_value = 4.0*  , *head_bias = False*  , *device = None*  , *dtype = None* ) [source](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.8.0/torch/nn/modules/adaptive.py#L20) 
:   Efficient softmax approximation. 

As described in [Efficient softmax approximation for GPUs by Edouard Grave, Armand Joulin,
Moustapha Cissé, David Grangier, and Hervé Jégou](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04309)  . 

Adaptive softmax is an approximate strategy for training models with large
output spaces. It is most effective when the label distribution is highly
imbalanced, for example in natural language modelling, where the word
frequency distribution approximately follows the [Zipf’s law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law)  . 

Adaptive softmax partitions the labels into several clusters, according to
their frequency. These clusters may contain different number of targets
each.
Additionally, clusters containing less frequent labels assign lower
dimensional embeddings to those labels, which speeds up the computation.
For each minibatch, only clusters for which at least one target is
present are evaluated. 

The idea is that the clusters which are accessed frequently
(like the first one, containing most frequent labels), should also be cheap
to compute – that is, contain a small number of assigned labels. 

We highly recommend taking a look at the original paper for more details.

#### Post Training Static Quantization 

Post Training Static Quantization (PTQ static) quantizes the weights and activations of the model. It
fuses activations into preceding layers where possible. It requires
calibration with a representative dataset to determine optimal quantization
parameters for activations. Post Training Static Quantization is typically used when
both memory bandwidth and compute savings are important with CNNs being a
typical use case. 

We may need to modify the model before applying post training static quantization. Please see [Model Preparation for Eager Mode Static Quantization](#model-preparation-for-eager-mode-static-quantization)  .

I'm not sure what you're trying to do here. You've got two different things happening at once - you're trying to train a model, but you're also trying to find a learning rate. These are two separate tasks, so it's not clear why you'd want them to happen simultaneously. In fact, they might interfere with each other, which would explain the errors you're seeing.

The first thing you should do is separate these two tasks. Train your model normally, then use the `lr_find()` method to find a good learning rate. Once you've found a good learning rate, you can retrain your model using that learning rate.

Here's some sample code showing how to do this:

```
# Train the model normally
learn.fit_one_cycle(1)

# Find a good learning rate
learn.lr_find()

# Plot the results
learn.recorder.plot(suggestion=True)

# Retrain the model using the suggested learning rate
learn.fit_one_cycle(1, max_lr=suggested_rate)
```

The problem here is that `lr_find` tries to create multiple workers to speed up the computation. However, it seems like you're trying to run this on Windows, which doesn't support multiprocessing out of the box. You can either switch to Linux or MacOS, or you can try to install the `spawn` backend by adding

```
if __name__ == "__main__":
    ...
```

at the beginning of your script. This will make sure that the multiprocessing backend is only loaded when the script is actually executed, but not when imported as a module.

Today, PyTorch supports the following backends for running quantized operators efficiently: 

* x86 CPUs with AVX2 support or higher (without AVX2 some operations have inefficient implementations), via *x86* optimized by [fbgemm](https://github.com/pytorch/FBGEMM)  and [onednn](https://github.com/oneapi-src/oneDNN)  (see the details at [RFC](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/83888)  )
* ARM CPUs (typically found in mobile/embedded devices), via [qnnpack](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/main/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qnnpack)
* (early prototype) support for NVidia GPU via [TensorRT](https://developer.nvidia.com/tensorrt)  through *fx2trt* (to be open sourced)

#### Note for native CPU backends 

We expose both *x86* and *qnnpack* with the same native pytorch quantized operators, so we need additional flag to distinguish between them. The corresponding implementation of *x86* and *qnnpack* is chosen automatically based on the PyTorch build mode, though users have the option to override this by setting *torch.backends.quantization.engine* to *x86* or *qnnpack* .

Note that `index`  and `src`  do not broadcast.

I'm not familiar with A2C but I can answer your questions about how gradient computation works in general.

In order to compute the gradients of some function `f` w.r.t. its input `x`, you need to define an objective function `g(x) = f(x)^2`. Then you can use any gradient-based optimization method (e.g., SGD, Adam, etc.) to minimize `g`.

For example, let's say we want to compute the gradient of `f(x) = x^3` w.r.t. `x`. We can do it as follows:

```
import torch

# Define the function
def f(x):
    return x ** 3

# Define the objective function
def g(x):
    return f(x) ** 2

# Create a tensor for which we want to compute the gradient.
x = torch.tensor([1.0], requires_grad=True)

# Compute the objective value
y = g(x)

# Compute the gradient
y.backward()

print(x.grad)
```

The output will be `[6.]` because the derivative of `f(x)` w.r.t. `x` is `3 * x ^ 2` and at `x=1` it equals `3`.

The difference is that `nn.init.xavier_uniform` returns the initialized tensor, while `nn.init.xavier_uniform_` modifies the input tensor in-place.

Be aware that `fan_in`  and `fan_out`  are calculated assuming

My model reports “cuda runtime error(2): out of memory” 
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

As the error message suggests, you have run out of memory on your
GPU. Since we often deal with large amounts of data in PyTorch,
small mistakes can rapidly cause your program to use up all of your
GPU; fortunately, the fixes in these cases are often simple.
Here are a few common things to check: 

**Don’t accumulate history across your training loop.** By default, computations involving variables that require gradients
will keep history. This means that you should avoid using such
variables in computations which will live beyond your training loops,
e.g., when tracking statistics. Instead, you should detach the variable
or access its underlying data. 

Sometimes, it can be non-obvious when differentiable variables can
occur. Consider the following training loop (abridged from [source](https://discuss.localhost:8000/t/high-memory-usage-while-training/162)  ): 

```
total_loss = 0
for i in range(10000):
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    output = model(input)
    loss = criterion(output)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    total_loss += loss

```

Here, `total_loss`  is accumulating history across your training loop, since `loss`  is a differentiable variable with autograd history. You can fix this by
writing *total_loss += float(loss)* instead.

Firstly, let's look at your example:

```

Now, if we take the negative mean of these values, we get:

```

# 0.3465736
```

Which is not equal to 8.05904769897461.

However, if we use the `from_logits=True` argument, then we get:

```

which outputs:

```
[0.        0.6931472]
```

and taking the negative mean gives us:

```

# 0.3465736
```

which is now equal to 8.05904769897461.

So, the difference between the two methods is whether or not the input has already been passed through a softmax function. If it has, then you should pass `from_logits=True`, otherwise you shouldn't.

I think you're misinterpreting what `scipy.interpolate.interp1d` does.

The documentation says:

> Return a 1-D piecewise linear interpolator to a set of data points.
>
> From the docs:
>
> > **Parameters:**  
> > * **x** – 1-D sequence of floats. Must be sorted if kind=‘linear’.
> >
> > * **y** – N-D array of float. y[i] corresponds to the data point at x[i]. If y contains multiple variables then each column represents one variable.
> >
> > * **kind** – str or int, optional. Specifies the kind of interpolation as a string (`‘linear’, ‘nearest’, ‘zero’, ‘slinear’, ‘quadratic, ‘cubic’`) or as an integer specifying the order of the spline interpolator to use.
> >
> > * **axis** – int, optional. Specifies the axis of y containing the data points for which to compute the polynomial fit. Default is 0.
> >
> > * **copy** – bool, optional. If True, make copies of x and y, else only references are used. Defaults to True.
> >
> > * **bounds_error** – bool, optional. If True, raise ValueError when x is outside of the range of x (where extrapolation is required). If False, extrapole value of y using a constant line which is a linear function of x outside range of x.
> >
> > * **fill_value** – array-like, optional. Value to use outside of bounds of independent variable. If None, then fill_value is set to NaN. If not specified, use partial least squares method to predict the value at the out-of-bound point(s).

So it's basically saying that given a list of points `(x,y)` it will create a linear function between those points. So if you have a single point `(0,0)` and another point `(1,1)` it will create a straight line between those points. This means that if you try to get the value of the function at `x=0.5` it will give you `0.5`.

What you seem to be doing is creating a linear function between `-1` and `1` and then trying to get the value of the function at `0`. But since your function is linear it will just give you `0`, because that's exactly where the line crosses the `x` axis.

If you want to map the values from `[0,1]` to `[-128,127]` you need to create a linear function between those points. You can do so by defining a function that takes a number `x` and returns `(-128 + 127*x)`. That way, if you pass `0` to the function it will return `-128` and if you pass `1` it will return `127`. And if you pass `0.5` it will return `0`.

In other words, you don't need to use `scipy.interpolate.interp1d` at all. You can simply define a function that maps the values from `[0,1]` to `[-128,127]` and use that function instead.

The main difference is that `torch.no_grad()` will not only detach tensors, but also disable all autograd hooks and graph building (e.g., for computing higher-order derivatives). This can be useful if you want to avoid unnecessary computations.

The key principle is to prevent the division by zero operation from being recorded in the computation graph, rather than masking its results after the fact. This ensures that autograd only computes gradients through valid operations. 

This behavior is important to keep in mind when working with operations that might produce `inf`  or `nan`  values, as masking the outputs does not prevent the problematic gradients from being computed.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

There are several mechanisms available from Python to locally disable gradient
computation: 

To disable gradients across entire blocks of code, there are context managers
like no-grad mode and inference mode.
For more fine-grained exclusion of subgraphs from gradient computation,
there is setting the `requires_grad`  field of a tensor.

evaluation mode ( `nn.Module.eval()`  ), a method that is not used
to disable gradient computation but, because of its name, is often mixed up with the three.

I'm not sure if you're asking about the specific error message you're seeing, or if you're asking more generally about how to handle version mismatches between different packages.

In general, it's best practice to specify your dependencies in a way that makes it easy to reproduce your environment exactly. The most common way to do this is by using a requirements.txt file (or similar) which lists out all of the packages you need along with their exact versions. You can then install them all at once using pip:

```
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

This ensures that everyone who uses your code will have the same versions of each package installed. If you want to make it even easier to replicate your environment, you can use a virtualenv or conda environment. These tools create isolated environments where you can install packages without affecting other projects on your machine. To create a conda environment based on your requirements.txt file, you could do something like this:

```
# Create a new conda environment called "my_env"
conda create -n my_env python=3.6

# Activate the environment
source activate my_env

# Install all of the packages listed in requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

If you're working with TensorFlow, there are a few extra steps you'll need to take to ensure that everything works correctly. In particular, you should always install TensorFlow first because many other packages depend on it. Here's an example requirements.txt file that should work for you:

```
tensorflow==2.2.0
transformers==3.0.2
pytorch==1.4.0
torchtext==0.5.0
```

To install TensorFlow, you'll need to use the conda-forge channel instead of the default conda channel. This tells conda to look for TensorFlow in the conda-forge repository rather than the default Anaconda repository. You can do this by adding `-c conda-forge` to your conda install command:

```
# Install TensorFlow using the conda-forge channel
conda install -c conda-forge tensorflow==2.2.0
```

Once you've done this, you should be able to load your saved model without any issues.

I'm not sure what you're asking. The first part of your question seems to be asking about the difference between `nn.CrossEntropyLoss()` and `F.cross_entropy()`. In general, you would use either one interchangeably, since they are just different ways of calling the same function. However, `nn.CrossEntropyLoss()` is a module, while `F.cross_entropy()` is a function. So, if you want to use the loss function as part of a larger network, you would use `nn.CrossEntropyLoss()`, whereas if you just want to compute the loss without creating a new module, you could use `F.cross_entropy()`. For more information, see <https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/nn.html#crossentropyloss>.

The second part of your question asks about the error message:

> RuntimeError: Expected object of scalar type Long but got scalar type Float for argument #2 'target'

This means that the `target` tensor has the wrong data type. It needs to be of type `LongTensor`, but instead it's of type `FloatTensor`. To fix this, you need to convert the `target` tensor to the correct data type. One way to do this is to use the `.long()` method:

```python
loss = loss_fn(pred_output, targets.long())
```

Alternatively, you could use the `.type()` method:

```python
loss = loss_fn(pred_output, targets.type(torch.LongTensor))
```

For more information, see <https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/tensors.html#tensor-types>.
